documents.unit: Student Handbook, Academic Honor Code and Academic Dishonesty (Baseline Policy on Generative AI Use in Student Work)
documents.title: The Academic Honor Code and Academic Dishonesty (includes Baseline Policy on Generative Artificial Intelligence Use in Student Work)
documents.summary: The student handbook honor code includes a baseline policy: all student work must be generated by students, and AI use not explicitly permitted by the instructor is academic dishonesty (cheating). Instructors may permit AI for specific assignments if stated in writing, permitted use must be cited, and sanctions run from course failure with probation to suspension or expulsion.
documents.stance_why: The baseline says "Unless explicitly permitted by the instructor, the use of AI tools for any part of any academic exercise ... constitutes Academic Dishonesty (cheating)" and "the default assumption is that AI is not permitted." AI is banned unless permitted, so restrict rather than delegates: the university itself sets the default while letting instructors open exceptions.

units.why: The opening expectation that all work "will be generated by students themselves" at every stage sets the baseline that students produce their own work; P19 fits because the point is authorship, while the explicit ban comes in the next sentences.
units.anchor: will be generated by students themselves

units.why: This defines generative AI as "any technologies that can autonomously produce text, images, code, media, translations", which sets what the policy covers, so P61 with modality informs.
units.anchor: any technologies that can autonomously produce text, images, code, media, translations, or other content

units.why: Naming "GitHub Copilot" among examples brings code assistants into scope; the main job of the sentence is scope-setting, but P07 is chosen over P61 because it is the passage that explicitly lists tools including an IDE assistant (the definition sentence itself is P61).
units.anchor: Examples include but are not limited to Grammarly, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DALL·E, GitHub Copilot, and
units.policy: Examples include but are not limited to Grammarly, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DALL·E, GitHub Copilot, and Slidesgo

units.why: Excluding "basic spelling and grammar correction tools" from the AI definition is a scope boundary about what counts as AI, so P61.
units.anchor: basic spelling and grammar correction tools (e.g., those embedded in standard word processors) to be
units.policy: basic spelling and grammar correction tools (e.g., those embedded in standard word processors) to be AI

units.why: "Unless explicitly permitted by the instructor, the use of AI tools for any part of any academic exercise" is dishonesty, a default ban unless permitted; P01 fits the default rule, and the later silent-syllabus sentence is coded separately as P06.
units.anchor: Unless explicitly permitted by the instructor, the use of AI tools for any part of
units.policy: Unless explicitly permitted by the instructor, the use of AI tools for any part of any academic exercise submitted for evaluation

units.why: The same sentence says such use "constitutes Academic Dishonesty (cheating)", a classification into integrity processes (P36), kept separate from the default ban (P01) because it is a distinct rule.
units.anchor: constitutes Academic Dishonesty (cheating).

units.why: Listing "using AI to generate ideas, outlines, titles, or drafts" as dishonest means brainstorming is banned by default; P19 fits (AI producing material for the work) better than P15, which is the permissive brainstorming type.
units.anchor: using AI to generate ideas, outlines, titles, or drafts;

units.why: Banning "using AI to summarize course readings" prohibits a study-aid use; P14 covers only permitted study aids and P19 covers producing submitted work, so neither fits and this is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: using AI to summarize course readings addressed in the assignment;
units.uncovered_note: Prohibits using AI to summarize course readings addressed in the assignment (a prohibited study-aid use, not producing submitted work).

units.why: "submitting AI-generated text or media as one's own" is the standard ban on AI-produced submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated text or media as one’s own;

units.why: "using AI to complete problem sets, coding tasks, or data analysis" bans AI-produced code and solutions as graded work, P19; this is the unit most relevant to computing.
units.anchor: using AI to complete problem sets, coding tasks, or data analysis;

units.why: "having AI edit or revise written work" bans AI editing of graded work, a checking use rather than generating; P21 (no AI to proofread or check graded work) fits better than P19.
units.anchor: having AI edit or revise written work.

units.why: "allows another person or entity — including an AI system — to assist with their work, without authorization" treats an AI like another person whose unauthorized help is dishonesty; P45 fits the analogy, while P36 is not chosen since the point is the equivalence.
units.anchor: allows another person or entity — including an AI system — to assist with their
units.policy: allows another person or entity — including an AI system — to assist with their work, without authorization

units.why: "in the case of knowingly using AI when prohibited, it is cheating" classes knowing prohibited use as cheating, an integrity classification, P36.
units.anchor: in the case of knowingly using AI when prohibited, it is cheating

units.why: "outsourcing any part of the academic process to AI tools" is named alongside purchasing work as dishonesty, so AI may not do any part of the process: P19.
units.anchor: outsourcing any part of the academic process to AI tools

units.why: "Individual faculty members may choose to be more restrictive" lets each instructor tighten the baseline, delegating stricter rules to the instructor: P04.
units.anchor: Individual faculty members may choose to be more restrictive than above

units.why: "may choose to permit the use of generative AI tools for specific assignments or purposes" lets instructors open exceptions per assignment, P04.
units.anchor: Individual faculty members may choose to permit the use of generative AI tools for specific
units.policy: Individual faculty members may choose to permit the use of generative AI tools for specific assignments or purposes

units.why: Permissions "must be clearly stated in the course syllabus or on the assignment prompt", requiring instructors to put AI expectations in writing: P09.
units.anchor: must be clearly stated in the course syllabus or on the assignment prompt;

units.why: Permissions "must define the extent and nature of permitted use (e.g., brainstorming only, coding assistance, citation help)" asks instructors to scope permitted uses; P09 (state expectations) fits and P05 does not since no named tiers are defined.
units.anchor: must define the extent and nature of permitted use (e.g., brainstorming only, coding assistance, citation
units.policy: must define the extent and nature of permitted use (e.g., brainstorming only, coding assistance, citation help);

units.why: Permissions "may differ from one assignment to another within the same course" confirms assignment-level variation, P04.
units.anchor: may differ from one assignment to another within the same course.

units.why: "In the absence of a clear statement granting permission, the default assumption is that AI is not permitted" is exactly the rule for a silent syllabus: P06.
units.anchor: In the absence of a clear statement granting permission, the default assumption is that AI
units.policy: In the absence of a clear statement granting permission, the default assumption is that AI is not permitted.

units.why: "should not assume that permission to use AI on one assignment implies blanket permission for the course" says permission does not carry over: P11.
units.anchor: Students should not assume that permission to use AI on one assignment implies blanket permission
units.policy: Students should not assume that permission to use AI on one assignment implies blanket permission for the course.

units.why: "students must: Clearly cite and attribute the AI tool used" requires acknowledging permitted AI use in the submission, P24.
units.anchor: Clearly cite and attribute the AI tool used;

units.why: "Describe the nature of its use" asks for how the tool was used (e.g. "used ChatGPT to generate initial outline"), a detail of the citation, so P25.
units.anchor: Describe the nature of its use

units.why: "use an accepted academic citation format (e.g., APA, MLA)" sets the citation format; P24 is the disclosure requirement, and P25 is not chosen since no tool or prompt details are demanded in this line.
units.anchor: Follow any course-specific citation guidelines or use an accepted academic citation format (e.g., APA, MLA).

units.why: "Failure to properly attribute AI use — even when permitted — constitutes a breach of academic honesty" makes nondisclosure itself the violation: P28.
units.anchor: Failure to properly attribute AI use — even when permitted — constitutes a breach of
units.policy: Failure to properly attribute AI use — even when permitted — constitutes a breach of academic honesty.

units.why: Permitted but improperly cited AI use "may ... constitute plagiarism, fabrication, or cheating", an integrity classification, P36.
units.anchor: When permitted but improperly cited, AI use may, depending on the circumstances, constitute plagiarism, fabrication,
units.policy: When permitted but improperly cited, AI use may, depending on the circumstances, constitute plagiarism, fabrication, or cheating.

units.why: "When not permitted, it is cheating (and ... may include fabrication as well)" restates the classification of unauthorized AI use and adds fabrication, so a separate P36 unit.
units.anchor: When not permitted, it is cheating (and depending upon circumstances, may include fabrication as well).

units.why: The cheating section sends readers with AI questions to the Baseline Policy, pointing to the university-level AI rule; P56 fits as a reference to the institution framework.
units.anchor: For questions regarding the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (“AI”), refer to the Baseline Policy
units.policy: For questions regarding the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (“AI”), refer to the Baseline Policy on Generative Artificial Intelligence Use in Student Work below.

units.why: "Faculty members should state, in advance, their policies and procedures concerning examinations and other academic exercises" requires advance communication of rules, which governs AI rules as well: P09.

units.why: For exams, "any external assistance ... is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the instructor" sets a closed default on assessments; AI is not named here but this is the exam rule for outside help, so P22.

units.policy: should assume that any external assistance (e.g., books, notes, calculators, conversations with others) is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the instructor

units.why: "it will be the student's responsibility to raise the question with the instructor" makes students ask when unsure whether work is their own: P10.

units.why: "Academic departments and programs, at their option, may further clarify this general definition in writing" lets units add their own written rules, delegating to departments: P04.
units.anchor: Academic departments and programs, at their option, may further clarify this general definition in writing

units.why: "A violation of the department's or program's statement shall be considered a violation of the academic dishonesty policy" makes unit rules enforceable through integrity processes: P36.

units.policy: A violation of the department’s or program’s statement shall be considered a violation of the academic dishonesty policy of the University as a whole.

units.why: "Ignorance of University policy concerning academic dishonesty shall not be a defense" holds students accountable for knowing the rules; P29 is the closest accountability type.
units.anchor: Ignorance of University policy concerning academic dishonesty shall not be a defense in any conduct
units.policy: Ignorance of University policy concerning academic dishonesty shall not be a defense in any conduct board proceeding.

units.why: The first-offense sanction "failure in the course and probation through tenure" is a concrete penalty stated in advance (P37), applying to AI misuse because unauthorized AI use is dishonesty.
units.anchor: failure in the course and probation through tenure; or

units.why: "failure in the course and suspension for one or more semesters or expulsion" for second offenses escalates penalties by offense, P37.

units.why: "The University reserves the right to change requirements, policies, rules, and regulations without prior notice" says policies may change; it is generic and not AI-specific, and P54 is the closest type.

documents.summary: Faculty-facing page from the Provost and Dean of the Faculty stating that AI use in teaching is an individual faculty choice. It asks faculty to be clear with students, lists ITS and CLTR support resources, and warns against entering confidential data into AI tools.

units.anchor: is a faculty member’s individual choice.

units.anchor: Individual faculty approaches as to whether AI is incorporated into their pedagogy vary considerably
